@MikeAlhayek I notice you have raised a large number of similar PRs over multiple repos; these PRs appear to be based on the incorrect assumption that every use of `?.Length == 0` (or similar) is automatically incorrect. As I have tried to express at length over in [SE.Redis](https://github.com/StackExchange/StackExchange.Redis/issues/2764) / [PR](https://github.com/StackExchange/StackExchange.Redis/pull/2765), this syntax is neither right nor wrong, but changing the intent to something else is *almost certainly* wrong, unless there is a specific example scenario described. I'm going to strongly suggest you close all of those PRs, and only redo them if you are very sure, based on a fully considered example, that the `?.Length` usage is *actually incorrect*.

issue_context.title: Invalid Zero Length check expression
comments: These cases are not invalid - they are intentionally *not* handling null in this case.

Seeing your proposed changes in the PR, I would say that most of them don't really change the behavior in any way since they have preliminary explicit null checks (which begs the question on usefulness of null-coalescing operator in those cases).

For example, this change also doesn't really change anything since `?.` evaluates to `default` if the operand is null. The only thing changed is style.

```diff
- if (metadataConstraints?.Count == 0)
+ if (metadataConstraints == null || metadataConstraints.Count == 0)
```

Some changes do have observable behavioral changes, but I suspect that the original behavior is intended. For example, here null meaning "default" seems pretty reasonable for me.

```diff
- bool isDefaultImplementedInterfaces = implementedInterfaces?.Length == 0;
+ bool isDefaultImplementedInterfaces = implementedInterfaces != null && implementedInterfaces.Length == 0;
```

> For example, this change also doesn't really change anything since `?.` evaluates to `default` if the operand is null. The only thing changed is style.

This is incorrect. `?.` with value type will result in `(T?)null` instead of `(T?)default`. So `?.Count == 0` really means `!= null` **&&** `.Count == 0`.

> > For example, this change also doesn't really change anything since `?.` evaluates to `default` if the operand is null. The only thing changed is style.
> 
> This is incorrect. `?.` with value type will result in `(T?)null` instead of `(T?)default`. So `?.Count == 0` really means `!= null` **&&** `.Count == 0`.

You're right. I assumed `metadataConstraints` to be a reference type here.

> I assumed `metadataConstraints` to be a reference type here.

It's not related to `metadataConstraints`. It's the result type of `Count` (int) being value type. The result type of `?.` is the same as `ResultType?`, which will be nullable value type when `ResultType` is value type.

> > I assumed `metadataConstraints` to be a reference type here.
> 
> It's not related to `metadataConstraints`. It's the result type of `Count` (int) being value type. The result type of `?.` is the same as `ResultType?`, which will be nullable value type when `ResultType` is value type.

I see. Can't believe how I did't already know that.

> I noticed many invalid expression when checking for a zero elements in a collection

Noticed where? I'm trying to understand what action is being requested with this issue. Do you see incorrect comparisons in this repo? Are you suggesting an analyzer? Are you suggesting the compiler is buggy? Thanks.

review_comments:
This case is valid, and does catches the hypothetic case when the received json value is `{ "result": { "value": { "tabs": null }}}` with explicit null literal.

However, since `Value<JArray>()` is a method instead of property, it's nullability information isn't considered preserved between calls. A valid expression would be `is null or { Count: 0 }`, but it may be too niche for a hypothetic case.

This code is in test suite, not production. It's not meaningful to be defensive for every possible situation.
The behavior is explicit and well known for these cases with `!= null && Length == 0`. We are not interested in changing them into more verbose form.

`?.Length == 0` strictly equals to `!= null` and `Length == 0`. This doesn't change anything.
This case is intentional to *not* handle null. It can also be simple written as `stringValue == ""`.
This case is incorrect. Nulls are explicitly accepted from other constructors. Note that nullable annotations are NOT enabled for this project.
